View in browser                 Damian Paletta   After a Week of Turmoil, Can the White House Lock It Down?   Plus, Putin wants a summit with Trump and Xi over Ukraine, and a billionaire couple pours in cash to reshape the Democratic Party     ERIC LEE/GETTY IMAGES   Good morning. With Kimberly Guilfoyle and Katie Zacharia, the White House had two messy exits last week. And then late Friday, President Trump essentially shelved a bipartisan law that aimed to put tough constraints on Russia, vexing some Republicans . It all happened in a pre-midterm window when politicians normally go out of their way not to cause a ruckus. Well, there wasn’t just one ruckus but three.

   Two weeks to go now until the voters determine control of Congress for Trump’s final two years in office. He is hopscotching the country trying to shore up GOP Senate seats. Republicans are certainly sweating it, though there are so many close races (even in blue states, like Michigan) that the Senate outcome is very much up in the air. Still, more drama at the White House isn’t helping the messaging in the final sprint.

   I just returned after sneaking off for a long weekend with my wife to hike in Sedona, Ariz., for our 21st anniversary. It’s breathtaking there. On Saturday, after a long trek around Bell Rock, we went to breakfast at the Coffee Pot (famous for its omelets, of which there are 101 varieties!). And sure enough, a group of protesters marched right by. (You can hike, but you can’t hide, I suppose). The group consisted of maybe 100 people, mostly senior citizens, including a woman in a Statue of Liberty costume on stilts. They were holding signs like “No Kings” and protesting against “Tyranny.”

   I stopped to talk to some of the organizers on the way back to my car. They were rabble-rousing, feeling part of something bigger, aware that Sedona is a bit of a blue pebble in a gigantic red rock pile. I asked if this protest felt bigger than ones in the past, and they said it was hard to tell. Some of the protesters were tourists. But this protest was one of scores held around the country. That gave them hope.

   Toward the end of the chat, one protester asked me where my wife and I went to dinner the night before. When I told the protester where, she muttered, “Tourist trap!”

   “I’m a tourist!” I responded. 

   “You should talk to the locals!” she said back to me.

   “That’s what I’m doing!”

   For even more of our midterms coverage, episodes 1 and 2 of our podcast series tracking the youth vote are out now.

   This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       People and Policies I’m Watching   Volatility in France: French leaders are trading blame after a weekend of rioting swept the country.

   Trump’s Monday: Trump is scheduled to sign an executive order at 11 a.m. ET, with first lady Melania Trump. After two policy meetings, the president will travel to Kansas to speak at a rally near Wichita.

       What I’m Following     IGOR IVANKO/AFP/GETTY IMAGES   Putin asks Trump and Xi for a meeting to decide Ukraine’s fate. Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed that he, Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping meet next month to talk about ending the Russia-Ukraine war on terms friendly to Moscow. Such a summit—one without the involvement of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky—would be unprecedented and send alarm bells ringing in European capitals and beyond.

   Meet the power couple pouring in cash to Democrats. Hedge-fund billionaires Steve and Sue Mandel have quietly poured at least $20 million into political, policy and media projects that are challenging the Democratic establishment and could reshape party politics for years to come. The Mandels are the chief funders of the group Majority Democrats, a year-old outfit that has become a proving ground for ambitious young Democratic lawmakers who don’t consider themselves part of the rising far left.

   Trump staffers are lawyering up in case Democrats win midterms. From cabinet secretaries to midlevel staffers, people who work for Trump are calling law firms in search of legal advice as they brace for an avalanche of investigations next year if Democrats take one or both houses of Congress in the midterms. Lawyers say the inquiries signal unease that Democrats will investigate everything from alleged pay-to-play pardons, to the Kennedy Center renovation and Donald Trump Jr. wedding.

       What Else Is Happening   • Democratic Socialists of America leaders are working with their endorsed candidates to pressure Hakeem Jeffries on progressive priorities.

   • Pennsylvania will offer a glimpse into whether Democrats in midterms can overcome their main weakness : the loss of blue-collar voters.

   • Dr. Sean Barbabella​, Trump’s primary physician, is among the few officials with complete knowledge of Trump’s health and one of a handful responsible for what the public knows about it.

   • Trump, pressing ahead amid a legal battle, said his overhaul of a public golf course in Washington, D.C., would begin in mid-November.
